prompt.en: At the operating frequency, cable A loses 0.05 dB/m over a 30 m route. Cable B loses 0.08 dB/m over a 12 m route. Which has less total attenuation, ignoring connector loss?

text.en: A, because its loss per metre is smaller.

feedback.en: That ignores route length. A totals 0.05 x 30 = 1.5 dB.

text.en: B, because its shorter route gives 0.96 dB rather than 1.5 dB.

feedback.en: Multiply each per-metre figure by its actual length before comparing.

text.en: Both, because a matched cable has no attenuation.

feedback.en: A good match does not remove conductor and dielectric loss.

text.en: A, because dividing loss per metre by length gives the total.

feedback.en: Total dB loss accumulates with length; it is multiplied, not divided.

explanation.en: A lower per-metre loss does not guarantee a lower total when the routes differ.

prompt.en: With antenna and cable unchanged, a desk tuner lowers the SWR seen by the radio. A meter at the antenna end of the main cable shows no change. What does that show?

text.en: The desk tuner has removed the main cable's heating loss.

feedback.en: The remote measurement does not show the load mismatch changing, and matching at the desk does not remove cable loss.

text.en: The lower radio-end reading shows that a larger fraction of power is now absorbed by the antenna.

feedback.en: The reading describes the radio side of the tuner. It does not measure power absorbed at the unchanged antenna or establish reduced main-line loss.

text.en: The tuner changed the impedance presented to the radio, not the antenna-end match.

feedback.en: The two measurements refer to different parts of the system. A radio-end match can improve while the antenna-side cable remains mismatched.

text.en: The remote meter probably needs recalibration because the radio-end match is now the reference for the entire line.

feedback.en: The measurements are on different sides of a matching network. Their disagreement alone is not evidence that the remote meter needs recalibration.

explanation.en: Use measurement position to distinguish a transformed radio load from a changed antenna match.

prompt.en: Replacing damaged lossy coax with low-loss cable improves received signals, but station-end SWR rises. Which interpretation should be tested before undoing the repair?

text.en: The better reception is sufficient evidence to treat the higher SWR as a calibration error.

feedback.en: Reception and match are separate observations. Improved reception does not establish a calibration error.

text.en: The old cable was more efficient because its SWR display was lower.

feedback.en: A lower station-end reading can result from attenuation, not greater efficiency.

text.en: The higher SWR is stronger evidence of heating loss than the cable's lower attenuation figure.

feedback.en: SWR is not a direct measurement of heat loss. Lower attenuation can reveal a reflection that was previously hidden by loss.

text.en: The new cable returns more reflected energy to the meter, revealing a mismatch the old loss hid.

feedback.en: Lower attenuation can improve delivery and reception while exposing more of the antenna-end reflection.

explanation.en: Do not use a low SWR reading caused by loss as a reason to keep an inefficient cable.
